extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and practitioners referencing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on how to examine patent applications and determine compliance with statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103), including search, claim construction, and communication of rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution / initial comprehensive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application. Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deficiencies should be explained clearly, particularly when they serve as a basis for a rejection. Whenever practicable, examiners and patent reexamination specialists should indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. A failure to follow this approach can lead to unnecessary delays in prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully develop non-prior-art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a rejection not based on prior art is proper (lack of adequate written description, enablement, or utility, etc.), such rejection should be stated with a full development of the reasons rather than by a mere conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a full explanation of the reasons supporting the rejection and, where practicable, indicate ways to overcome the rejection to avoid unnecessary prosecution delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what invention is sought to be patented
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must begin examination by determining what, precisely, the inventor has invented and is seeking to patent, and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the complete specification, including the detailed description, any specific embodiments disclosed, the claims, and any specific, substantial, and credible utilities asserted for the invention. After understanding the invention, conduct a prior art search and determine statutory compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and understand any asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention as a whole must be useful. Examiners should review the application to identify any asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete disclosure should contain some indication of the practical application for the claimed invention (why the applicant asserts the invention is useful). The utility statement must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand why the applicant asserts the invention is useful. The application may describe more than one utility, but only one is necessary; alternatively, the examiner may rely on contemporaneous art establishing a well‑established utility. See MPEP §2107 for utility examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review detailed disclosure and specific embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description exemplifies the invention, explains how it relates to prior art, and explains the relative significance of various features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should (A) determine the function of the invention (what it does when used as disclosed), and (B) determine the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application. Applicants can assist by preparing applications that clearly set forth these aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define property rights — perform thorough claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny to identify the boundaries of protection sought and how claims relate to the inventor's indicated invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine scope by thoroughly analyzing the claim language before checking statutory compliance. Begin by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation (steps for processes; structures/materials for products). Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe it, in all cases — including means-/step-plus-function language. Consider grammar and plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill; some language may raise questions as to limiting effect (see list A–F in MPEP: preamble/field of use, 'adapted to/for', 'wherein/whereby', contingent limitations, printed matter, terms with functional language). Do not dissect a claim into elements and evaluate in isolation; consider the claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of a properly construed claim is defined by the terms that limit the scope of the claim when given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure may be express, implicit, or inherent. Means- (or step-) plus-function limitations are given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with corresponding structures/materials/acts described in the specification and their equivalents. Use specification to determine intended meaning but do not read positive limitations from the specification into the claim that the claim does not itself impose. See MPEP §2111 and related sections for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a thorough prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to evaluating patentability, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention if there is reasonable expectation the unclaimed aspects may be later claimed. Account for structure/materials described in the specification and their equivalents corresponding to claimed means-/step-plus-function limitations, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§2181–2186. See MPEP §§904–904.03 for how to conduct a search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility and utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 has been interpreted as imposing four requirements: (i) only one patent may be obtained for an invention; (ii) inventor(s) identification requirements; (iii) the claimed invention must be eligible for patenting; and (iv) the claimed invention must be useful (have utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold inquiry, but even if eligible the claim must also satisfy 102, 103, and 112. Examiners should avoid focusing solely on 101 to the detriment of other statutory requirements. See MPEP §§2104, 2106, 2107 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — definiteness and claiming what inventor regards as invention
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) contains two distinct requirements: (A) that the claims set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention, and (B) that the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is deficient under the first requirement when evidence outside the application shows the inventor regards the invention as different from what is claimed. An application fails the second requirement when claims do not set out and define the invention with reasonable precision and particularity; definiteness must be analyzed in light of the disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill. See MPEP §§2171–2173 and related subsections for particulars, including 112(f) scope and related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a): written description, enablement, best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) contains three separate requirements: (A) adequate written description, (B) enablement, and (C) best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the specific standards for each: written description must show possession; enablement must permit a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation; best mode requires examining whether inventor possessed a best mode at filing and whether it is disclosed sufficiently to practice it. See MPEP §§2163–2165 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2163 for standards, typical circumstances where issues arise, burden on the examiner, changes to claim scope, and relationship to new matter and amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex experimentation is not undue if persons of skill routinely engage in it. Consider tests of enablement, undue experimentation factors, working and prophetic examples, predictability of the art, and quantity of experimentation. See MPEP §2164 and subsections (2164.01–2164.08) for evaluation details including examples in chemical, biological, and computer programming cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining compliance with the best mode requirement requires a two‑prong inquiry: (1) at filing, did the inventor possess a best mode for practicing the invention; and (2) if so, does the written description disclose the best mode so a person of ordinary skill in the art could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2165 et seq. for considerations. Best mode deficiencies are not commonly encountered in examination because supporting evidence is seldom in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (novelty and nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing for 102 and 103 begins with comparing claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art. If no differences are found, the claim lacks novelty (35 U.S.C. 102). If differences are found, assess whether those differences render the claim nonobvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art (35 U.S.C. 103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If differences exist, assess them in light of knowledge of a person of ordinary skill to determine obviousness. Use MPEP §§2131–2146 (anticipation/102) and §§2141–2146 (obviousness/103) for guidance including scope/content of prior art, level of ordinary skill, prima facie obviousness, reasonable expectation of success, and consideration of applicant rebuttal arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure prima facie case before imposing rejections; clearly communicate bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Once analyses under statutes are complete, examiners should review proposed rejections and their bases to confirm that a prima facie case of unpatentability exists. Only then should any rejection be imposed in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions, and reasons which support them. Examiners should use the applicable form paragraphs in office actions to state the basis for objections or rejections to reduce misunderstanding as to grounds of objection or rejection. See MPEP guidance on forming and supporting rejections.
